newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Klima shaken by Bank Austria no-confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: Klima shaken by Bank Austria no-confidence vote.

text.p: Austrian Chancellor Viktor Klima survived a no-confidence vote over the privatisation of Bank Austria on Thursday but his People's Party coalition partners were grudging in their support for the embattled Social Democrats.
"We are remaining in government out of a sense of responsibility for Austria, not out of loyalty to the Social Democrats," People's Party deputy Guenter Stummvoll said.

The no-confidence motion, sponsored by the far-right Freedom Party, was defeated by 115 votes to 35. The ballot came at the end of an extraordinary debate on the Social Democrats' handling of the sale of the nation's top bank.
The Freedom Party had demanded clarification on when the government learned Germany's Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale had acquired first refusal on a majority stake in state-owned Bank Austria.
The bank was privatised on the general understanding that it would remain under Austrian control.

Klima, a former finance minister, stood accused of backing Bank Austria's acquisition of rival Creditanstalt in January in the knowledge that WestLB already had first option on Vienna's 45.15 percent Bank Austria voting stake.
Vienna city hall, like parliament, is dominated by the Social Democrats.

"Klima has misled parliament and the public by claiming he knew nothing of the deal with WestLB at the time of Creditanstalt's privatisation," Freedom Party deputy Helmut Haigermoser said ahead of the vote.
"The nation can no longer tolerate this chancellor," he continued.
Klima, who was due to fly to Sweden later on Thursday, insisted he knew nothing of the first refusal deal, struck in 1995 between Vienna City holding company AVZ and WestLB.
"I was not informed," Klima told deputies during the debate, adding: "This search for scapegoats is damaging to Austria's banks and economy."
The Freedom Party was joined in criticising the chancellor by conservative coalition partner the People's Party.

Conservative ministers have expressed outrage that Social Democrats, including Vienna mayor Michael Haeupl and Finance Minister Rudolf Edlinger, kept quiet about the WestLB agreement. Edlinger replaced Klima at the treasury in January and was Vienna finance officer at the time of the deal.
"The coalition parties have succeeded in building up mutual trust in recent months. The last thing we want is to lose that trust," Economy Minister Hannes Farnleitner said.
He has called on the government to annul Creditanstalt's privatisation if WestLB upholds its first refusal.
The suggestion sent a shiver through the financial sector, which saw the six-year privatisation of Creditanstalt bring the government to the brink of collapse at the start of the year.
Then the People's Party agreed only reluctantly to allow Social Democrat-dominated Bank Austria to take over the country's most conservative bank.

"I have the impression there is a deliberate attempt to do us damage," Austrian news agency APA quoted Randa as saying. The bank was expected to announce the share price for a three billion schillings capital increase on Thursday or Friday.
Analysts said the preference share issue should be a success based on purely financial data but noted political disputes over Austria's closed banking sector tended to distract from fundamentals.
Bank Austria preferred shares closed eight schillings down at 416 in a moderately firmer Vienna market.
